pedagogy.summary: Recognising, finding, naming, and writing 1/3, 1/4, 2/4, and 3/4 of a length, shape, set, or quantity. Two ideas mature here: the DENOMINATOR tells how many equal parts to share the whole into, and the NUMERATOR tells how many of those parts to take (so non-unit fractions like 3/4 are three of the quarter-parts). Fractions of a discrete SET (1/3 of 12 counters) sit alongside fractions of continuous shapes/lengths.
bestPractices: Find a unit fraction by sharing the whole into denominator-many EQUAL parts and taking one; build the non-unit fraction as repeated unit fractions (3/4 = three quarters)
Move between continuous (shade 3/4 of a rectangle) and discrete (1/3 of 12 counters) models
For a set, share into denominator-many equal GROUPS (not groups of that size), then take numerator-many groups
Name and write alongside the action so notation is tied to meaning
Keep the whole explicit and fixed while working
keyRepresentations: A set of counters shared into equal groups (denominator groups; take numerator)
A rectangle/strip partitioned and shaded (e.g. 3 of 4 parts for 3/4)
A length/number line marked into equal parts
Unit-fraction tiles combined to build a non-unit fraction
commonMisconceptions: Reading the denominator as the group SIZE, not the number of groups (1/3 of 12 -> makes groups of 3)
Treating a non-unit fraction like a unit fraction - taking only ONE part for 3/4
Number-vs-quantity: sharing an equal COUNT of unequal-sized items rather than equal amount
Losing track of the whole, or ignoring leftover items when a set doesn't divide evenly

learn.summary: Year 2 pupils (ages 6-7) recognise, find, name, and write the fractions 1/3, 1/4, 2/4, and 3/4 of a length, shape, set of objects, or quantity. Two linked ideas mature: the DENOMINATOR says how many EQUAL parts (or equal groups) to share the whole into, and the NUMERATOR says how many of those parts to take, so a non-unit fraction like 3/4 is three of the quarter-parts, not a single piece. Work moves between continuous wholes (shading part of a rectangle or marking a length) and discrete sets (a third of 12 counters), always keeping the whole explicit and fixed.

activities.title: Fraction-of-a-set bench: share into equal groups, then take some
feedback: If a child makes groups OF three for 1/3 of 12, stop and re-share: the 3 means THREE equal groups; put all 12 into three hoops and take one group (4), not a group of three.
If a child reports 3/4 of 12 as 3, they took only one quarter: build 3/4 as three of the quarter-groups - the numerator counts how many quarters to take, giving 9.
If groups are made unequal, point out that fractions need EQUAL parts before any part can be named.
When toggling to the shaded strip, confirm the child sees the same answer two ways (e.g. 3 of 4 shaded parts match the 3 of 4 groups).
activities.rationale: Finding a fraction of a set or shape is a partition-and-select action; sharing into denominator-many equal groups and selecting numerator-many makes both numbers meaningful, and building 3/4 by taking numerator-many quarter-parts reflects the source principle that non-unit fractions are composed of unit fractions. A live set-and-shape tool with a denominator dial, equal-group enforcement, group selection, and a continuous/discrete toggle can make the share-then-take mechanism and immediate feedback concrete; these are optional interaction examples, not required mechanisms - counters, hoops, and drawn strips achieve the same actions.
sourceClaims: Problems sharing one object yield unit fractions; multiple-object sharing yields non-unit fractions, which are composed of unit fractions (3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4)
learnerActions: Put out 12 counters as the whole. To find 1/3, share ALL 12 into 3 equal groups (one group per hoop) and take one group - record '1/3 of 12 = 4'.
To find 3/4, share all 12 into 4 equal groups (3 in each) and take THREE of the four groups - record '3/4 of 12 = 9'.
Say aloud 'the bottom number is how many equal groups; the top number is how many groups I take' as you act it out.
Re-show the same fraction as a shaded strip or rectangle divided into the denominator and shaded to the numerator, to see the continuous and discrete versions side by side.

Check a non-dividing case: with a different set of items that does not share evenly (for example 10 counters into 3 groups), notice the leftover. It means the groups cannot all be equal with whole items, so that fraction of the set cannot be found exactly with whole counters (1/3 of 10 is not 3).
activities.intendedInsight: The denominator sets how many EQUAL groups/parts to make; the numerator says how many of those to take - so 3/4 is three quarters, not one piece, and the same fraction describes both a set and a shape.

activities.title: Build a non-unit fraction from unit-fraction parts
feedback: If the child takes only one part for 3/4, count the quarters together: one quarter, two quarters, three quarters - the top number tells how many to take.
If they lose track of the whole, restate what the whole is and re-share it into equal parts before taking any.
activities.rationale: The source principle that non-unit fractions are composed of unit fractions supports building 3/4 as 1/4+1/4+1/4; naming and writing alongside the action ties notation to meaning.
sourceClaims: Problems sharing one object yield unit fractions; multiple-object sharing yields non-unit fractions, which are composed of unit fractions (3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4)
learnerActions: Find a unit fraction first: share the whole into denominator-many equal parts and take one (e.g. 1/4 of a strip, or 1/4 of 12 counters = 3).
Build 3/4 by repeating that quarter three times (1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4), counting the quarters taken.
State the link: 3/4 means three of the four equal parts, so it is three unit-fractions put together.
Write the fraction next to the action each time so the notation stays tied to the meaning.
activities.intendedInsight: A non-unit fraction is repeated unit fractions: 3/4 is three quarters, built by taking one quarter three times.

activities.title: Same number or same amount? Guarding against the count-vs-quantity trap
feedback: If the whole is an amount of stuff and a child makes equal-count groups of unequal-sized pieces, colour-cue quantity versus count and ask again 'same number of things, or same amount?'
Confirm that for identical counters equal count and equal amount coincide, but for mixed sizes an equal count can leave the amounts unequal.
activities.rationale: The IES guide notes children confuse the number of things shared with the quantity shared, especially with unequal-size items; surfacing this distinction directly - and defining fair sharing as equal amount - targets the misconception.
sourceClaims: Children confuse the number of things shared with the quantity shared, especially with unequal-size items (Roadblock 1.3)
learnerActions: Compare a third of 12 LARGE counters with a third of 12 TINY counters: is the NUMBER of things the same? Is the total AMOUNT the same?

With a mixed set of big and small pieces of the same stuff (e.g. pieces of food to share fairly), check whether equal-COUNT groups also hold an equal AMOUNT. When the whole is an amount of stuff, amount, not count, is what fair sharing must make equal. Exact equal amounts may not be possible without cutting pieces.
Discuss aloud: 'same number of things, or same amount?' to separate the two ideas.
activities.intendedInsight: When the whole is an amount of stuff, fair sharing means giving each share an equal AMOUNT. With identical counters, counting gives equal amounts, but with unequal-sized pieces an equal count is NOT the same as an equal amount, so children must check the amount, not just the number of things. When the question is about the number of objects in a set, the count is what matters.

activities.title: Fraction of a length on a number line or ruler
feedback: If parts along the length are unequal, re-mark so all parts are equal before naming the fraction.
If the child treats 2/4 and 1/4 as the same, count the parts taken: 2/4 takes two of the four equal parts.
activities.rationale: The curriculum requires fractions of a length as well as of shapes and sets; moving between a length, a shape, and a discrete set builds transfer.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils recognise, find, name, and write fractions 1/3, 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 of a length, shape, set of objects, or quantity
learnerActions: Mark a length or strip into denominator-many equal parts and find 1/4 of it.
Compare this with 1/4 of a set of counters: how are the two alike (share into 4 equal parts, take one) and unlike (a length is continuous; counters are separate things)?
Find 2/4 and 3/4 of the same length and notice 2/4 is halfway and 3/4 is three of the four equal parts.
activities.intendedInsight: The same share-then-take rule applies to lengths as to sets and shapes, so fractions transfer across continuous and discrete wholes.

activities.title: Naming and writing practice (recognition and recall check)
feedback: If '1/3 of 12 = 3' is chosen, re-share into THREE equal groups: each group has 4, so a third is 4; a group OF three is a different thing.
Use the denominator-as-group-size wrong answer as a discussion point, not a penalty.
activities.rationale: Naming, matching, and fill-in tasks suit recognition and recall of fractions of amounts and can embed a targeted wrong-answer trap; note that recognition-only responses check recall and do not by themselves elicit the independent sharing action, so pair them with the hands-on bench work.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils recognise, find, name, and write fractions 1/3, 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 of a length, shape, set of objects, or quantity
learnerActions: Match fractions (1/3, 1/4, 2/4, 3/4) to correctly shaded pictures of shapes and sets.
Complete statements such as '3/4 of 12 = __' and '1/3 of 12 = __'.
Spot and reject a tempting wrong answer such as '1/3 of 12 is 3' (which reads the denominator as a group size).
activities.intendedInsight: Fractions of amounts can be named, matched, and written once their meaning is secure, consolidating the link between notation and quantity.

constraints: Fractions require EQUAL parts/groups; share the whole into denominator-many equal parts before taking any.
For a set, share into denominator-many equal GROUPS (not groups of that size), then take numerator-many groups.
Keep the whole explicit and fixed throughout a task.
Non-unit fractions (2/4, 3/4) are repeated unit fractions - take numerator-many parts, not one.

A reference poster or labelled image is reference-only: tapping to highlight parts-taken versus total-parts can support naming but does not have the child do the sharing, so it is a scaffold, not a replacement for partition-and-select practice.
Recognition and matching tasks assess and consolidate naming/writing but do not on their own require the learner to construct the partition; pair them with hands-on sharing.
When a set does not divide evenly, address any leftover explicitly rather than ignoring it.

When the whole is an amount of stuff (e.g. food or material), fair sharing makes the AMOUNT equal; equal COUNT only guarantees this for identical items, so distinguish count from amount when items differ in size. When the whole is the number of objects in a set (e.g. 1/3 of 12 counters), the fraction refers to the count.
Compare fractions as fixed quantities: 2/4 of 12 takes two of the four equal parts, 1/4 takes one; never describe the denominator rule as 'flipping'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy entry asserted '3D adds nothing' and treated a live interactive bench as uniquely ideal; these are catalog-fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and have been softened to affordance-based framing. Hands-on counters, drawn strips, and number lines are equally valid media.
The legacy 'conversation: poor - built by doing' framing was not propagated as a universal claim; discussion ('same number or same amount?') is retained as useful alongside doing.

Arithmetic self-checked: 1/3 of 12 = 4 (three equal groups of 4); 3/4 of 12 = 9 (four equal groups of 3, take three); 1/4 of 12 = 3; 2/4 of 12 = 6; 4/4 of 12 = 12. The wrong answers '1/3 of 12 is 3' and '3/4 of 12 is 3' are retained only as explicitly-labelled misconception traps, never as valid answers.
The probe '4/4 of the 12 counters' correctly resolves to all 12 (the whole); covered by the whole-fixed constraint and preserved worked values.

Editor change: the curriculum source claim was removed from Activity 1, whose rationale is about the partition-and-select mechanism (a topic-level attribution there). It remains in Activities 4 and 5, where the rationale is about length-transfer and naming/writing, which the claim directly supports.

Editor change: Activity 3's intendedInsight and feedback were tightened so fair sharing is defined as equal AMOUNT, with equal count presented only as the method valid for identical items; this avoids reinforcing the count-vs-quantity misconception it targets. No fresh source verification was performed.

probeDeeper: Show me 2/4 of the 12 counters - is that more or less than 3/4?
If I had 12 big counters and 12 tiny ones, is a third of each the same NUMBER? The same AMOUNT?
Find 1/4 of this strip (a length) - how is that like, and unlike, 1/4 of the counters?
assess.correctAnswer: One-third of 12: share into 3 equal groups (4 in each) -> 4. Three-quarters of 12: share into 4 equal groups (3 in each) and take 3 groups -> 9. The bottom number (denominator) says how many equal groups/parts to make; the top number (numerator) says how many of those parts to take.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the denominator as the group SIZE, not the number of groups - for 1/3 of 12 makes groups of 3
errorPatterns.nextMove: Emphasise the 3 means THREE equal groups; share all 12 into three hoops and take one.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports 1/3 of 12 as 3 (or makes 4 groups of 3 and is unsure which is the answer)

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats a non-unit fraction like a unit fraction - takes only ONE part for 3/4
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build 3/4 as three of the quarter-groups; the numerator counts how many quarters to take.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports 3/4 of 12 as 3 (one quarter) instead of 9

errorPatterns.pattern: Number-vs-quantity: shares an equal COUNT of unequal-sized items rather than an equal amount
errorPatterns.nextMove: Colour-cue quantity vs count (IES); ask 'same number of things, or same amount?'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: With mixed big/small items, makes equal-count groups regardless of amount

responseLevels.gap: Shares by the wrong thing (groups OF n), or takes one part for a non-unit fraction; treats the two numbers as unconnected.
responseLevels.full: Finds 1/3, 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 of sets, lengths, and shapes by sharing into denominator-many equal parts and taking numerator-many, explains the role of each number, and transfers between continuous and discrete wholes.
responseLevels.partial: Finds unit fractions of a set correctly but stumbles on a non-unit fraction (3/4), or works on a shape but not on a discrete set.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put out 12 counters. Ask: 'Find one-third of these counters, then find three-quarters of these counters, and tell me how you worked out each one.' Then ask: 'Why do you share by the bottom number, and what does the top number tell you to do?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: One-third forces the child to make the denominator-many EQUAL GROUPS (a child who makes groups OF three reports the wrong thing). Three-quarters forces them to take NUMERATOR-many parts (a child who treats it like a unit fraction takes only one part and says 3). The two items together separate a secure part-whole reading of the notation from a shallow one.
